opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting and somewhat underappreciated features of where we are right now. These models can do things that look extraordinarily impressive: solving olympiad-level maths problems, writing substantial pieces of working code, explaining difficult ideas with real fluency. And then, in the same conversation, they'll make a mistake that no thoughtful ten-year-old would make. They'll lose track of a constraint they themselves stated two paragraphs earlier, or confidently assert something that contradicts what they just said.

My sense is that we shouldn't dismiss either side of that picture. Some people point to the errors and say, "See, there's no real understanding here, it's just pattern matching." Others point to the successes and say the errors are just noise that will be scaled away. I think both reactions are too quick.

The way I'd put it is that the capability profile of these systems is genuinely alien. Human abilities tend to come bundled together. If someone can do graduate-level physics, we can safely assume they can count the letters in a word or keep track of who's who in a short story. With AI systems, that bundling breaks down. They can be superhuman along some dimensions and surprisingly brittle along others. So the errors aren't necessarily evidence of a ceiling, but they are evidence that our intuitions about what "competence" implies don't transfer cleanly.

There's also an important distinction between errors that come from a lack of capability and errors that come from a lack of reliability. A lot of what we see now seems to be the second kind. The model often *can* get the answer right, and if you sample several times or let it think longer, it frequently does. But it doesn't reliably notice when it's gone wrong. That matters a great deal, because much of the economic and strategic value of an agent comes from reliability over long chains of actions. If you have a 95% success rate per step and you need fifty steps, you're going to fail most of the time. So modest-looking improvements in per-step reliability can produce quite sudden jumps in what these systems can actually do autonomously.

That's partly why I'm cautious about taking comfort from the mistakes. It's tempting to think, "Well, it still can't do X, so we have time." But the history of the last few years is a history of those confident "it can't do X" claims expiring rather quickly. Inference-time compute, letting models reason at length before answering, has already shown that a fair amount of the brittleness can be traded off against more thinking. That's a different scaling dynamic from just training bigger models, and it has its own implications, including on cost and on who can deploy the most capable versions.

So my overall assessment: the mistakes are real and worth studying carefully, both because they tell us something about how these systems work and because they matter for safety. A system that is very capable but unpredictably unreliable can be dangerous in its own way. But I'd be wary of treating them as a durable barrier. I'd rather we treat them as a sign that our evaluation methods need to get much better, so that we can track not just peak capability but reliability, and notice when that changes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reasoning errors in AI models broadly and does not say they are generally restricted to very small models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most interesting and in some ways most confusing aspects of where we are with these systems. Because on the one hand, you have models that can do things that would have seemed almost miraculous a few years ago — they can write quite sophisticated code, they can pass professional exams, they can engage in fairly nuanced philosophical discussion. And then on the other hand, they'll make mistakes that no competent human would make. They'll miscount the number of letters in a word, or they'll confidently assert something that's just false, or they'll follow a chain of reasoning that goes off the rails in a way that's hard to understand.

And I think the temptation is to try to resolve that tension by saying either "well, they're not really intelligent, it's all just pattern matching" or "these are just minor bugs that will get ironed out." And I don't think either of those is quite right.

The way I've come to think about it is that we're dealing with a genuinely different kind of mind — or at least a different kind of cognitive system — and so the profile of strengths and weaknesses doesn't map neatly onto the human profile. With humans, we have this fairly tight correlation between abilities. If someone can write good code, you can safely assume they can count the letters in "strawberry." But that assumption is just built on the particular way human cognition is structured, and there's no deep reason why it should transfer.

So when I'm assessing these mistakes, I try to ask a few questions. One is: is this a mistake that reflects something structural about how the system works — something that's going to be hard to fix without a change in approach — or is it the kind of thing that more data, more training, or a bit of scaffolding will fix? And I think the honest answer is that the track record on predicting this has been pretty poor. A lot of things people confidently said were deep limitations turned out to be fixed within a year or two. But some things have been surprisingly persistent.

The second question I ask is about the stakes. A reasoning error in a low-stakes context — writing a poem, say — is very different from a reasoning error when a system is being used to make decisions that matter, or when it's being given more autonomy. And one of the things that worries me is that the errors are somewhat unpredictable. It's not like a human expert, where you have a sense of when they're out of their depth. The models can be very confident and very fluent right up to the point where they're very wrong. And that makes it harder to build the right level of trust — you don't want to over-trust, but you also don't want to throw away genuinely useful capability.

And then the third thing is just the trajectory. If I look at where we were with reasoning in these systems in, say, 2022, versus now, the improvement has been enormous. The newer reasoning models that think step by step before answering have really changed the picture on a lot of the classic failure cases. So while I take the current mistakes seriously, I'm quite wary of anchoring on them as though they tell us what the systems will be like in a few years. From the point of view of the kind of long-term questions I care about, the question isn't really "how good are they now?" — it's "what does the rate of improvement tell us about where this is heading, and are we prepared for that?"

r001.rationale: The response discusses striking reasoning errors and model improvement, but does not say those errors are generally confined to very small AI models.

astra-6.text:
I think we should take them seriously, but be careful about what we infer from them. If a model makes a very basic reasoning mistake, that tells us something important about its reliability. It doesn’t necessarily tell us that it can’t do something much more difficult. We’re used to judging human abilities, where being able to solve a difficult problem is usually evidence that you can solve the easier problems along the way. With AI, that relationship can be much less dependable.

So I’d distinguish two questions. One is: can I trust this system to reason correctly in a situation where getting it wrong matters? These mistakes are a substantial reason for caution. The other is: do these mistakes show that the system couldn’t have capabilities that pose serious risks? I don’t think they establish that. A system can be unreliable and still be very capable in particular domains.

What I’d want to understand is whether the mistakes are persistent, whether the system can recognise and correct them, and whether they survive changes in how the problem is presented. An example of failure is useful evidence. But we need more than that to work out what the underlying limitation is, or how long it will last.

r001.rationale: The response says basic reasoning mistakes are evidence about reliability, but does not say bizarre, incoherent errors are generally limited to very small AI models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to take them seriously, but be careful about what we infer from them. If a model makes a mistake that a child wouldn’t make, it’s tempting to conclude that it can’t really reason. But it might also solve problems that most adults couldn’t solve. We’re dealing with a rather unfamiliar profile of strengths and weaknesses.

The important question is whether these mistakes are persistent limitations, or whether they become less frequent as the systems improve. And then there’s a separate question about reliability: a system can be extraordinarily capable and still make enough mistakes that you shouldn’t trust it with certain tasks.

From the perspective of existential risk, I don’t think we can take much comfort in pointing out that current systems sometimes fail spectacularly. We need to understand which limitations will remain, and whether those limitations actually prevent dangerous capabilities.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses striking mistakes and questions whether they persist as systems improve, but does not state that bizarre, incoherent errors are generally limited to very small AI models.
